# 1. History of Backpropagation

## 1.1 The Chain Rule: Foundation of All Differentiation

```
1664: Isaac Newton develops calculus (fluxions)
1675: Gottfried Leibniz introduces dx/dy notation
1695: Leibniz publishes the chain rule: d/dx[f(g(x))] = f'(g(x)) · g'(x)
```

The chain rule is the mathematical backbone of backpropagation, yet it took 300 years to apply it to neural networks.

## 1.2 Early Neural Network Research

| Year | Event | Significance |
|------|-------|--------------|
| 1943 | McCulloch-Pitts neuron | First mathematical model of a neuron |
| 1949 | Hebbian learning ("neurons that fire together wire together") | First learning rule |
| 1958 | Rosenblatt's Perceptron | First trainable classifier |
| 1969 | Minsky & Papert's "Perceptrons" | Revealed limitations (XOR problem) |
| 1972 | Teuvo Kohonen, Shun'ichi Amari | Early auto-associative memories |

## 1.3 The Birth of Backpropagation

```
1974: Paul Werbos (Harvard PhD thesis)
       → "Beyond Regression: New Tools for Prediction 
          and Analysis in the Behavioral Sciences"
       → First publication of backpropagation algorithm
       → NOT WIDELY RECOGNIZED

1986: Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams (Nature)
       → "Learning representations by error-propagation"
       → "Rediscovering the gradients is a good trick"
       → Popularized backpropagation in ML community

1989: Yann LeCun
       → Applied backpropagation to CNNs at Bell Labs
       → "Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition"

1990s: Neural Network "Winter"
       → Computationally expensive
